title: MCP Clients & Transports
summary: An MCP client is the piece inside a host that opens a session with a server, discovers its capabilities, and invokes tools on the agent's behalf. It reaches the server over a transport — stdio for a local subprocess, or HTTP with Server-Sent Events for a remote one — but the JSON-RPC messages are identical either way. You'll connect a client, list tools, call one, and wire discovered tools into an agent loop, noting that SDK client APIs churn even though the flow is stable.
nestedConcepts: wiring tools into the agent loop

subtopics.title: The client's job
subtopics.explanation: A client is the host-side half of one MCP session: it launches or dials a server, performs the initialize handshake, keeps the connection alive, and translates the agent's intentions into JSON-RPC calls. One client owns exactly one server session, so a host with three servers runs three clients. Seeing the client as a per-server session manager — not a global bus — is what makes multi-server hosts easy to reason about.
subtopics.example:
# One client == one server session. A host runs several.
clients = {}
clients["files"]    = MCPClient()   # session to the files server
clients["github"]   = MCPClient()   # separate session, separate process
clients["postgres"] = MCPClient()

# each client independently: connect -> initialize -> discover -> call
for name, c in clients.items():
    c.connect(name)          # opens ONE session
# the host multiplexes across clients; each owns just its own server.

subtopics.title: stdio vs HTTP/SSE transports
subtopics.explanation: A transport is just how bytes move between client and server. stdio launches the server as a local subprocess and pipes JSON-RPC over its stdin/stdout — ideal for local tools and dev. HTTP with Server-Sent Events (SSE) dials a remote server over the network, using SSE so the server can stream messages back. The key insight: the transport changes connection setup only; the JSON-RPC request/response shape above it is identical, so your tool-calling code doesn't care which one you picked.
subtopics.example:
# stdio: server runs as a LOCAL subprocess, JSON-RPC over pipes
local = MCPClient(transport="stdio", command=["python", "files_server.py"])

# HTTP/SSE: server is REMOTE, reached over the network
remote = MCPClient(transport="sse", url="https://tools.example.com/mcp")

# SAME calls regardless of transport -- only setup differs:
local.list_tools()
remote.list_tools()
# the JSON-RPC envelope above the transport is identical.

subtopics.title: Connecting and the initialize handshake
subtopics.explanation: Before any tool call, client and server perform an initialize exchange: the client announces its protocol version and capabilities, the server replies with its own, and they agree on a common ground. Only after this handshake are list/call methods valid. Treating initialize as a required first step — not an optional nicety — is what prevents version-mismatch bugs when SDKs on each side differ.
subtopics.example:
# The handshake precedes every other call.
async def open_session(client):
    await client.connect()          # transport is live
    info = await client.initialize(  # negotiate version + capabilities
        protocol_version="2024-xx-xx",
        client_info={"name": "my-host", "version": "1.0"},
    )
    # info.capabilities tells you what the server supports.
    # ONLY now are tools/list, tools/call, etc. valid.
    return info

subtopics.title: Discovering capabilities
subtopics.explanation: After initialize, the client asks the server what it offers — list its tools, resources, and prompts — and caches the result for the session. Each tool comes back with its name, description, and input JSON Schema, which is exactly what the agent needs to advertise the tool to the model. Discovery is dynamic: the host learns a server's abilities at runtime rather than hard-coding them, which is the whole point of a pluggable standard.

subtopics.title: Wiring server tools into the agent loop
subtopics.explanation: The payoff: feed the discovered tools to the model, let it choose one, and route that choice back through the client as a tools/call. The client returns the result, which you append to the conversation as an observation and loop again — exactly the reason→act→observe loop, with MCP supplying the 'act'. This wiring is what turns a catalog of servers into an agent that can actually use them.
subtopics.example:
# MCP supplies the 'act' step of the agent loop.
history = [{"role": "user", "content": goal}]
for _ in range(MAX_STEPS):
    step = llm(history, tools=model_tools)   # reason: model picks a tool
    if step.done:
        break
    # act: route the model's choice through the MCP client
    result = await client.call_tool(step.tool, step.args)  # tools/call
    # observe: feed the tool result back into context
    history.append({"role": "tool", "content": result.text})

foundations.overview: An MCP client is the host-side endpoint of a single server session. Its lifecycle is connect → initialize → discover → call. Connecting brings a transport online: stdio launches the server as a local subprocess and pipes JSON-RPC over stdin/stdout, while HTTP with Server-Sent Events dials a remote server and lets it stream responses back. Crucially, the transport only affects how the connection is established; the JSON-RPC envelope above it is identical, so the same tool-calling code works over either. After connecting, client and server run an initialize handshake to negotiate protocol version and capabilities — required before any list or call method is valid. The client then discovers the server's tools, resources, and prompts, each tool arriving with a name, description, and input JSON Schema that maps directly onto the tool format a model expects. Finally, the client is wired into the agent loop: discovered tools are advertised to the model, the model chooses one, the client executes it via tools/call, and the result is fed back as an observation. As always with MCP, the SDK client APIs shift between versions, but this connect-initialize-discover-call flow is the stable model to learn.
foundations.formalDefinition: An MCP client is a host-side component that maintains one stateful JSON-RPC session with a server over a chosen transport (stdio for a local subprocess, or HTTP/SSE for a remote endpoint). Its lifecycle is: establish the transport, perform an initialize handshake negotiating protocol version and capabilities, discover the server's tools/resources/prompts via list methods, and invoke them via call/read/get methods — feeding tool results back into the agent loop as observations.
foundations.whyItMatters: The client is where MCP meets the agent loop: it is the component that turns 'the model wants to call a tool' into an actual invocation and an observation. Because it isolates transport and session management from the model's reasoning, one agent can use local and remote servers interchangeably, and discovery lets it learn capabilities at runtime instead of hard-coding them — the practical mechanism that makes pluggable tools real.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of the client as a phone line to one server. stdio is an intercom to a device in the same building (a local subprocess); HTTP/SSE is a long-distance call to a remote office. Either way you speak the same language once connected. You dial (connect), exchange pleasantries and agree on a common protocol (initialize), ask what services they offer (discover), and then place requests (call). The agent loop is you deciding what to ask for next based on each answer.
foundations.performanceImpact: stdio has near-zero network latency and is ideal locally, while HTTP/SSE adds round-trip and connection overhead but enables remote/shared servers and streaming. Discovery is a one-time per-session cost you should cache rather than re-list each turn. In the loop, each tool call is a full round trip whose result becomes context tokens, so batching independent calls and returning concise results reduces both latency and downstream token cost.
commonUseCases: Connecting a local dev tool server over stdio
Dialing a shared remote server over HTTP/SSE
Discovering a server's tools at runtime and advertising them to the model
Routing the model's tool choice through the client inside an agent loop

commonMisconceptions.myth: The transport changes how you call tools.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Transport (stdio vs HTTP/SSE) only affects connection setup and byte movement. The JSON-RPC request/response shape and your tool-calling code are identical over either.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You can skip initialize and call tools directly.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The initialize handshake negotiates protocol version and capabilities and must complete before list/call methods are valid; skipping it causes version-mismatch and protocol errors.

commonMisconceptions.myth: One client can manage many servers.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A client owns exactly one server session. A host with multiple servers runs multiple clients and multiplexes across them; treating a client as a global bus leads to tangled session state.

codeLab.title: Build a session-guarded MCP client wrapper
codeLab.instructions: Implement a MiniClient class that models the MCP client lifecycle against an injected server object (the server exposes handle(method, params) -> dict). Requirements: (1) initialize() must call the server's 'initialize' method and set a ready flag, returning the server's response. (2) list_tools() must raise RuntimeError('not initialized') if initialize() has not been called; otherwise it calls 'tools/list' and returns the response's 'tools' list. (3) call_tool(name, arguments) must also guard on ready, call 'tools/call' with params {'name': name, 'arguments': arguments}, and return the text of the first content item (result['content'][0]['text']). Complete the class so the harness passes.
hints: Set self.ready = False in __init__ and flip it to True inside initialize().
Write a small _require_ready() helper that raises RuntimeError('not initialized') when self.ready is False, and call it at the top of list_tools and call_tool.
For call_tool, pass params={'name': name, 'arguments': arguments} and return res['content'][0]['text'].

theory.question: Walk through the MCP client lifecycle and explain how a client relates to servers in a host.
theory.directAnswer: A client owns one stateful session with one server and follows the lifecycle connect → initialize → discover → call. It establishes a transport, runs the initialize handshake to negotiate version and capabilities, lists the server's tools/resources/prompts, and then invokes them via call methods. A host with multiple servers runs multiple clients and multiplexes across them.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The host-side session manager for one MCP server connection, isolating transport and protocol state from the agent's reasoning.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Separating a per-server session into its own client keeps multi-server hosts tractable and lets transport and version negotiation live in one place instead of leaking into the loop.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: connect brings the transport online (stdio subprocess or HTTP/SSE endpoint); initialize negotiates protocol version/capabilities; list methods discover capabilities (each tool carrying name, description, input schema); call methods execute them and return content the loop uses as observations.

theory.whyImportant: This lifecycle is the concrete point where MCP integrates with the agent loop and where transport/version concerns are contained, which is what lets one agent mix local and remote servers safely.
theory.realWorldExample: An IDE assistant runs three clients — a stdio client for a local files server, and two HTTP/SSE clients for shared git and database servers — each independently initialized and discovered, all feeding the same agent loop.

followUps.question: Can one client hold two server sessions?
followUps.answer: No — one client is one session with one server. Multiple servers mean multiple clients that the host multiplexes across.

followUps.question: What happens if versions mismatch at initialize?
followUps.answer: The handshake surfaces the mismatch so the sides can negotiate a common protocol version or fail cleanly, rather than silently breaking on a later call.

theory.question: Compare the stdio and HTTP/SSE transports and explain when you'd choose each.
theory.directAnswer: stdio launches the server as a local subprocess and pipes JSON-RPC over stdin/stdout — lowest latency, ideal for local tools and development. HTTP with Server-Sent Events dials a remote server over the network and lets it stream responses back — right for shared or remote servers. The choice affects only connection setup and latency; the JSON-RPC message shape above the transport is identical.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The two standard ways an MCP client moves bytes to a server: local subprocess pipes versus a remote HTTP endpoint using SSE for server-to-client streaming.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Local tools want a zero-network, easy-to-spawn channel, while shared or hosted tools need a networked, streamable channel; one protocol over two transports covers both without changing the message layer.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: stdio spawns the server command and reads/writes framed JSON-RPC on its standard streams; HTTP/SSE opens an HTTP connection and uses an event stream so the server can push responses/notifications. The client's tool-calling code is unchanged across both.

theory.whyImportant: Understanding that transport is orthogonal to the message layer lets you develop against a local stdio server and deploy against a remote HTTP/SSE one with no change to your agent logic.
theory.realWorldExample: A team develops a data-tool server locally over stdio, then deploys the same server behind HTTP/SSE for the whole org; the agent code that lists and calls tools didn't change at all.

followUps.question: Why SSE rather than plain HTTP request/response?
followUps.answer: SSE lets the server stream multiple messages/notifications back over one connection, which suits MCP's asynchronous, long-lived session model better than one-shot requests.

followUps.question: Any security difference between the two?
followUps.answer: A remote HTTP/SSE server crosses a network boundary and needs auth, transport encryption, and access scoping, whereas a local stdio subprocess is bounded by the host machine — relevant when building a safe server.

scenario.question: Your agent connects to a remote MCP server over HTTP/SSE and every tools/call returns a 'method not allowed' style protocol error, even though the same server works locally over stdio. How do you diagnose it?
scenario.directAnswer: Check whether the initialize handshake actually completed on the remote connection before any call — a common cause is treating HTTP/SSE like a stateless request and skipping or losing the session, so the server rejects calls made outside an initialized session. Verify the client reuses one initialized session for subsequent calls and that protocol versions negotiated cleanly.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A session-state bug where transport differences expose a missing or dropped initialize/session step that stdio happened to hide.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Over stdio the subprocess session is implicitly long-lived; over HTTP/SSE it's easy to open a fresh connection per call or mishandle the session, so calls arrive without a valid initialized session.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Inspect the JSON-RPC traffic: confirm an initialize request/response precedes list/call on the same session, confirm the negotiated protocol version matches, and confirm the client isn't reconnecting per call. Fix by holding one initialized session and reusing it for all calls.

scenario.whyImportant: It reinforces that transport changes setup and session handling — not the message shape — so bugs that only appear remotely usually trace to session/handshake lifecycle, not the tool logic.
scenario.realWorldExample: Logs showed the HTTP client opened a new connection per tool call, so each call skipped the earlier initialize; pinning a single initialized session for the agent's run made the remote path behave exactly like stdio.

followUps.question: How would you confirm the handshake ran?
followUps.answer: Capture the JSON-RPC messages and verify an initialize request/response pair precedes any tools/list or tools/call on the same session id/connection.

followUps.question: Why did stdio hide the bug?
followUps.answer: The stdio subprocess is one persistent process/stream for the whole run, so the single initialize naturally covered every later call; the per-request HTTP pattern broke that assumption.

coding.question: Write a function that converts MCP-discovered tools into a provider tool format and runs one turn of an agent loop, given a model function and a client.
coding.thoughtProcess: Discovered MCP tools carry name, description, and input_schema, which I map onto the provider's {name, description, parameters} shape. I then ask the model for a step; if it wants a tool I route the call through the client, capture the text result, and return it as an observation dict so a caller can append it to history. Keeping this a single turn makes the reason→act→observe boundary explicit and testable.
lineByLine: to_model_tools maps each discovered MCP tool's name/description/input_schema onto the provider's expected tool shape.
run_turn first discovers and converts tools, then asks the model for one step.
If the step is done, it returns the final answer and stops — the loop's termination case.
Otherwise it routes the model's chosen tool through client.call_tool, the MCP 'act' step.
The tool result is wrapped as an observation dict (role 'tool') for the caller to append to history.
The __main__ block wires a fake client and model to show a single reason→act→observe turn end to end.
coding.timeComplexity: O(t) to convert t discovered tools, plus one model call and at most one tool call per turn.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(t) for the converted tool list.

followUps.question: How would you turn this into a full loop?
followUps.answer: Call run_turn repeatedly inside a bounded for-loop, appending each returned observation to history until a step comes back done or the step cap is hit.

followUps.question: Why cache the tool conversion?
followUps.answer: Discovery is stable within a session, so converting once and reusing avoids re-listing every turn, cutting latency and redundant round trips.

keyTakeaways: An MCP client owns one server session; a host with multiple servers runs multiple clients and multiplexes across them.
The client lifecycle is connect → initialize → discover → call, and initialize must complete before any list/call.
Transport (stdio for local subprocess, HTTP/SSE for remote) changes only connection setup — the JSON-RPC shape is identical.
Discovery returns each tool's name, description, and input JSON Schema, which maps directly onto the model's tool format.
In the loop, MCP supplies the 'act': the client executes the model's chosen tool and the result flows back as an observation.
